title: ABIMELECH NEARLY SLEPT WITH ANOTHER MAN’S WIFE WITHOUT KNOWING IT
paragraphs: ABIMELECH NEARLY SLEPT WITH ANOTHER MAN’S WIFE WITHOUT KNOWING IT
He thought Sarah was Abraham’s sister. Abraham had hidden the most dangerous part of the truth. Then God entered a pagan king’s dream with words that could make any man wake up trembling.
There are nights when sleep is an escape.
And there are nights when God meets a man inside his sleep and exposes something he never knew was happening.
Abimelech went to bed as a king.
He woke up knowing he had nearly become an adulterer.
Not because he had deliberately hunted another man’s wife.
Not because Sarah had introduced herself as married.
Not because Abraham had warned him.
Quite the opposite.
Abraham had said of Sarah:
“She is my sister.”
And Sarah had said of Abraham:
“He is my brother.”
Then Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for Sarah and took her into his household.
From his perspective, the situation apparently seemed legitimate.
Then God came.
Genesis 20:3 records one of the most terrifying interruptions in Scripture:
“But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night, and said to him, ‘Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man’s wife.’”
The Hebrew is startlingly direct:
הִנְּךָ מֵת
hinneka met
“Behold—you are a dead man.”
Then comes the reason:
וְהִוא בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל
vehi be'ulat ba'al
She is a woman belonging in the covenant of marriage to a husband—another man’s wife.
Imagine waking inside that dream.
Imagine discovering that something you believed was acceptable had placed you dangerously close to violating someone else’s marriage.
But this is where the story becomes even more remarkable.
Abimelech had not yet slept with Sarah.
Scripture is explicit about that.
“Now Abimelech had not come near her.”
So he answered God:

“Lord, will You slay a righteous nation also? Did he not say to me, ‘She is my sister’? And she, even she herself said, ‘He is my brother.’ In the integrity of my heart and innocence of my hands I have done this.”
And God did not dismiss his defense.
God confirmed it.
“Yes, I know that you did this in the integrity of your heart.”
But then God revealed something Abimelech could never have known on his own:
“For I also withheld you from sinning against Me; therefore I did not let you touch her.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
“I did not let you touch her.”
Abimelech could say, “I didn’t do it.”
But God could say, in effect, “And you need to understand why.”
That changes everything.
Because sometimes the sin you never committed is not evidence that temptation could never have conquered you.
Sometimes it is evidence that mercy stood between you and the edge.
Abimelech had integrity concerning what he knew.
Yet he was still walking toward disaster because he did not possess the whole truth.
And God stopped him.
That should humble every one of us.
How many doors did God close that you once complained about?
How many relationships fell apart that you begged Him to restore?
How many opportunities disappeared?
How many plans failed?
How many people suddenly walked away?
How many times did something inside you say, “Don’t go there,” and you never understood why?
We often thank God for the blessings He gives us.
Perhaps eternity will reveal that we should also thank Him for thousands of things He never allowed us to have.
The phone call that never came.
The relationship that never happened.
The temptation that lost its opportunity.
The secret meeting that got interrupted.
The door that mysteriously closed.
The person who rejected you.
The plan that collapsed.
The night that ended earlier than expected.
You called some of those moments disappointment.
Heaven may have called some of them mercy.
“For I also withheld you from sinning against Me.”
There is another detail here that we cannot ignore.
God did not merely describe adultery as sin against Abraham.
He said it would be sin “against Me.”
That is the terrifying seriousness of sin.
Sin wounds people, destroys trust, fractures families, corrupts consciences, and leaves consequences behind.
But ultimately sin is rebellion against God.
David understood this after his own catastrophic sexual sin. After adultery with Bathsheba and the orchestration of Uriah’s death, David cried:
“Against You, You only, have I sinned, and done this evil in Your sight.”
That does not mean Uriah and Bathsheba were irrelevant victims. It means David finally understood the vertical horror underneath the horizontal devastation.
Sin is ultimately against the God whose holiness we have violated.
And this is where Genesis 20 becomes uncomfortable for religious people.
Because the man being warned is Abimelech.
But the man who created the deception is Abraham.
Yes.
Abraham.
The man of faith.
The man God called.
The man who received promises.
The man whose faith would become one of Scripture’s great examples.
Abraham was afraid.
He believed the men of Gerar might kill him because of Sarah’s beauty, so he concealed the full nature of their relationship.
There was a technical element of truth in Abraham’s statement. Genesis 20:12 explains that Sarah was indeed his half-sister.
But a partial truth deliberately used to create a false impression can still deceive.
Abraham allowed Abimelech to believe something that was dangerously incomplete.
And suddenly the “man of God” does not look very heroic.
That matters.
Because Scripture does not airbrush its heroes.
The Bible is astonishingly willing to show us the embarrassing chapters.
Noah became drunk.
Jacob deceived.
Moses disobeyed.
David committed adultery and arranged a killing.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples argued over greatness.
And Abraham—the great patriarch of faith—acted out of fear and put another man in terrible danger.
Why preserve stories like this?
Because the Bible is not fundamentally a collection of stories about impressive human beings.
It is the revelation of a faithful God working through deeply flawed people.
The scandal is human sin.
The wonder is divine grace.
And grace does not mean God pretends sin does not matter.
Look at Abimelech.
God warned him.
God commanded him:
“Now therefore, restore the man’s wife.”
Grace did not rename adultery.
Grace prevented it.
Grace exposed the deception.
Grace demanded restoration.
Grace protected Sarah.
Grace confronted Abraham.
Grace spared Abimelech.
Grace brought what was hidden into the light.
That is biblical grace.
And perhaps somebody reading this has misunderstood grace because you thought grace meant Jesus simply overlooks what you are doing.
He does not.
The same Jesus who forgives sinners calls sinners to repentance.
The Gospel is not:
“God does not care about your sin.”
The Gospel is that God cared about our sin so profoundly that the Son of God entered our world to save sinners from it.
Jesus did not die so we could become comfortable hiding.
He died to bring us home.
And maybe that is why this story feels painfully personal.
Because most of us know what it feels like to hide behind a technically true sentence.
“I’m fine.”
Technically, you survived today.
But you are not fine.
“We’re just friends.”
Technically, perhaps nothing physical happened.
But your heart already crossed boundaries you would be terrified for your spouse to see.
“I only looked.”
“I never touched anybody.”
“Nobody knows.”
“It wasn’t technically lying.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“It’s just entertainment.”
“It’s only messaging.”
“It’s only flirting.”
“It’s only once.”
“It isn’t hurting anyone.”
Human beings are extraordinarily talented at constructing sentences that make darkness sound harmless.
Abraham did something painfully human.
He told enough truth to protect himself while withholding enough truth to endanger someone else.
And God dragged the hidden reality into the light.
What are you hiding behind?
Not what are you admitting publicly.
What are you hiding behind?
Because God sees beneath our carefully constructed explanations.
Hebrews 4:13 says:
“And there is no creature hidden from His sight, but all things are naked and open to the eyes of Him to whom we must give account.”
That verse should frighten hypocrisy.
But for the repentant sinner, it can also become strangely comforting.
Because the God who knows everything about you is the same God who sent Christ for sinners.
You do not have to manufacture a cleaned-up version of yourself before approaching Jesus.
He already knows.
The pornography.
The affair.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The bitterness.
The compromise.
The nights nobody knows about.
The thoughts you would never put on Facebook.
The version of yourself your church friends have never met.
He knows.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
“Repent therefore and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out.”
Blotted out.
Not managed.
Not cosmetically covered.
Not renamed.
Forgiven.
This is why Jesus Christ is infinitely greater than religious image management.
Religion says, “Make yourself look clean.”
Jesus says, “Come into the light.”
Religion teaches people how to hide scars.
Jesus shows His scars.
Religion whispers, “If people knew everything, they would leave you.”
At the cross, Christ demonstrates something staggering:
God knew everything.
And Christ came anyway.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after we erased our history.
“While we were still sinners.”
This does not minimize repentance.
It makes repentance possible.
You can stop hiding because there is grace for the person who comes honestly to Christ.
You can confess because Jesus already knows.
You can surrender because the One receiving your surrender was crucified for sinners and rose again.
You can walk away from secret sin because your identity does not have to remain chained to your worst chapter.
This is what the Gospel does.
It takes scandal and writes grace across the page.
Abraham failed.
God remained faithful.
Abimelech was endangered.
God intervened.
Sarah was placed in a vulnerable situation.
God protected her.
The situation was tangled with fear, deception, danger, and potential sexual sin.
God entered the mess.
And He did not merely observe it.
He acted.
That pattern reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Humanity did not climb its way back to God.
God came to us.
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
Jesus stepped into our wreckage.
He touched lepers.
He ate with sinners.
He welcomed the rejected.
He confronted hypocrites.
He forgave the repentant.
He carried a cross.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not the story of good people finally earning God.
It is the story of sinners who could never rescue themselves being offered redemption through Jesus Christ.
That is why your scandal does not have to become your final sentence.
Your failure does not have to become your name.
Your secret does not have to become your master.
Your past does not have authority to write your ending.
Jesus does.
But do not confuse that with permission to remain unchanged.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
The Christ who receives you says, “Follow Me.”
Maybe God is interrupting something in your life right now.
Maybe this article itself feels uncomfortable because there is something you already know needs to end.
Do not wait for destruction to convince you that conviction was mercy.
Do not wait until the affair destroys your marriage.
Do not wait until pornography reshapes the way you see human beings.
Do not wait until bitterness becomes your personality.
Do not wait until secret compromise becomes public catastrophe.
Do not wait until the thing you control begins controlling you.
Abimelech received a warning before the act.
That warning was mercy.
And perhaps somebody needs to understand this today:
Conviction is not God abandoning you.
Conviction may be evidence that God is calling you away from destruction.
The question is what you will do when the truth reaches you.
Abimelech acted.
Genesis tells us he rose early, summoned his servants, confronted Abraham, restored Sarah, and sought to make the situation right.
There is something powerful about that.
When truth arrived, he did not spend the next six months negotiating with it.
Somebody reading this has been negotiating with conviction for too long.
You know.
God knows.
And beneath all your explanations, you know that He knows.
So stop running.
Not toward shame.
Toward Christ.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Turn from the secret relationship.
Turn from pornography.
Turn from dishonesty.
Turn from bitterness.
Turn from spiritual pretending.
Turn from the identity you built without God.
Turn toward Jesus.
There is forgiveness in Him.
There is cleansing in Him.
There is a new life in Him.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to be painfully simple:
“Jesus, no more hiding.”
Not because typing three words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that God has exposed something in us becomes the first crack in the wall we have spent years building.
Let believers reading the comments pray instead of pretending none of us struggle.
Your testimony may become hope for a person who thinks change is impossible.
And please do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not as superstition. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. Salvation is by grace through faith, not by social-media activity.
Somebody may be one decision away from detonating a marriage.
Somebody may have convinced himself that secret sin is harmless.
Somebody may be ashamed to walk into a church but willing to read an article alone at 2:00 in the morning.
Somebody may need to discover that conviction is not the end of the story.
Jesus still saves.
Send this privately to the person you cannot stop thinking about while reading it.

Supporting Gospel work financially does not purchase salvation, earn God's favor, or prove that someone glorifies God. Christ purchased our redemption, and grace cannot be bought. But voluntary generosity, sharing biblical truth, and helping make discipleship resources available to others can certainly be ways believers choose to honor God and participate in Gospel ministry.
Look at yourself.
There may have been moments when you stood closer to destruction than you realized.
There may have been sins God prevented that you will never know about.
There may have been closed doors you resented that were actually mercy.
There may even be something God is stopping you from doing right now.
Listen.
Come into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the grace Christ purchased.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because the most astonishing part of Genesis 20 is not merely that a king almost slept with another man's wife without knowing it.
It is that God stepped between a human being and a sin he did not yet understand he was about to commit.
And perhaps one day, when we finally see our lives from heaven's side, some of our deepest worship will rise not only because of what God gave us...
…but because we finally discover what His mercy never allowed to destroy us.
Some of the doors you still call disappointments may one day be remembered as the places where mercy quietly stood between you and ruin.
